docs.text: EN ↔ ҚАЗ · 473 terms The words Technical Kazakh is still being decided in public. This is the set of choices this site makes, why it makes them, and what to avoid. If you teach or write in Kazakh, take it and argue with it. 01 How we write Kazakh here Keep the tool word, translate the concept Words the learner will type or see on screen stay as they are: git, prompt, agent, API, deploy, token, repo, frontend, backend, MCP, Claude Code. docs.text: EN ↔ ҚАЗ · 473 terms The words Technical Kazakh is still being decided in public. This is the set of choices this site makes, why it makes them, and what to avoid. If you teach or write in Kazakh, take it and argue with it. 01 How we write Kazakh here

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Keep the tool word, translate the concept
docs.text: Words the learner will type or see on screen stay as they are: git, prompt, agent, API, deploy, token, repo, frontend, backend, MCP, Claude Code. Words that have already settled into Kazakh are written in Cyrillic: агент, токен, модель, сервер, код, файл, промпт, репозиторий, коммит. Everything else gets a real Kazakh word: қолданба (app), тармақ (branch), біріктіру (merge), дерекқор (database), сілтеме (link), құпиясөз (password).

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Latin word + hyphen + Kazakh ending
docs.text: Attach the ending with a hyphen, never an apostrophe and never a space: GitHub-қа, git-те, Claude Code-ты, API-ге, LLM-ді, Vercel-ге. Choose the ending by how the word sounds, not how it is spelled: Claude is read [клод], so it behaves like a back-vowel word ending in a hard consonant, giving Claude-қа and Claude-та. When the reading is unclear (Gemini, production, CLI, IDE, README), drop the suffix and put a Kazakh descriptor noun after the name instead: CLI құралында, production ортасына, README файлын.

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Cyrillic loans take endings directly
docs.text: A word already written in Cyrillic needs no hyphen: промптты, токендер, серверге, репозиторийде, агентпен, модельдің. The hyphen belongs to Latin script and to acronyms only. Kazakh also never uses an apostrophe for this, the way Turkish does, so API-ге is right and the apostrophe form is not.

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Never suffix a command or a file name
docs.text: A command has to be typed character for character, so it never carries a Kazakh ending. Wrap it in a descriptor noun instead: write «npm install пәрменін орында», not «npm install-ды орында»; write «CLAUDE.md файлын аш», not «CLAUDE.md-ны аш». The same holds for file names, flags and anything shown as inline code.

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Address the learner as сен
docs.text: Learner-facing prose, tips and quiz feedback use сен: «Промптты нақтырақ жаз», «Жарайсың!». Buttons and menu items use the neutral infinitive, so the interface itself never has to choose a register: «Бастау», «Сақтау», «Кодты көшіру». Error messages use no second person at all and no exclamation mark: «Жүктеу мүмкін болмады», not «Сен жүктей алмадың». Prompts written to an AI are сен-form imperatives too, which is exactly the register the learner will be typing all day.

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Numbers and dates the Kazakh way
docs.text: Dates start with the year: «2026 ж. 22 қыркүйек»; the short form is 22.09.2026. Months and weekdays are lowercase. Time is 24-hour (19:00) and a range uses an en dash with no spaces (19:00–21:00). Decimals take a comma (3,5), thousands a non-breaking space (1 500), money the same (5 000 ₸). Percent has no space, 80%, and its ending takes a hyphen, «80%-ы». A noun after a numeral stays singular: «5 сабақ», «3 коммит», never «5 сабақтар». Ordinals written in digits take a hyphen: «1-қадам», «3-модуль». A version is written «2.3 нұсқасы».

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Drop the Russian calques
docs.text: Use қолданба not қосымша, жүктеп алу not скачать ету, параметрлер not настройкалар, құпиясөз not пароль, сілтеме not ссылка, түйме not кнопка, қалта not папка, пайдаланушы not юзер, әзірлеуші not разработчик, нұсқа not версия, әдепкі not по умолчанию, дерекқор not мәліметтер базасы. Never hang Russian verb endings on an English root: instead of закоммитить, запушить, пофиксить, задеплоить write «commit жасау», «push жасау», «түзету», «deploy жасау». And never use the Russian-flavoured spellings бэкенд, фронтэнд, деплой, вайб-кодинг: backend, frontend, deploy and vibe coding stay in Latin.

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Gloss the term once, then use the short form
docs.text: The first time a term appears on a page, give the Kazakh rendering with the English in parentheses: «Тармақ (branch) — кодтың жеке көшірмесі…». After that use whichever form is shorter and clearer, тармақ or branch. This rule applies per page, not per site, because most people arrive straight into one lesson from search. 02 Terms No term matches. Try part of the word.

docs.title: The words
docs.section: AI basics
docs.text: vibe coding → vibe coding stays in Latin Writing software by telling an AI in plain language what you want, then looking at what it built. Build your first app with vibe coding, but read the code yourself afterwards. avoid: вайб-кодинг artificial intelligence (AI) → жасанды интеллект (ЖИ) Technology that lets a computer do work that used to need human thinking. Working with AI is a skill every builder needs today, not a separate profession. also: ЖИ avoid: ИИ large language model (LLM) → үлкен тілдік модель (LLM) A program trained on huge amounts of text to predict what comes next, which is how it writes answers and code. Do not think of an LLM as a database: it does not look the answer up, it writes it. also: ҮТМ model → модель One trained AI program you can send a request to; each one differs in strength, speed and price. Pick a cheap model for simple tasks and a strong one for hard ones. token → токен The smallest piece a model actually reads and writes: a word, a part of a word, or a punctuation mark. Everything is counted in tokens: the price, the limits and the context window.

docs.title: The words
docs.section: AI basics
docs.text: tokenizer → токенизатор The part that cuts text into tokens; every model family has its own. tokenizer tax → токен салығы The extra cost of writing in a language the tokenizer handles badly: Kazakh text needs roughly two to four times more tokens than the same meaning in English. Write prompts and CLAUDE.md in English, keep Kazakh for what the user reads. also: tokenizer tax context window → контекст терезесі Everything the model can see at once: your instructions, the conversation, the files it read and its own reply. Anything outside the context window simply does not exist for the model. context → контекст All the information the model has in front of it at the moment it writes an answer. context rot → контексттің тозуы The fact that answers get less reliable as the input grows, even on easy questions. A long window does not fix context rot: start a fresh session for a new task. also: context rot temperature → температура A setting for how much randomness goes into choosing the next token: low means repeatable, high means varied. Keep it low for code, raise it for brainstorming. h

docs.title: The words
docs.section: AI basics
docs.text: allucination → галлюцинация Output that sounds right but is invented: a function that does not exist, a fake link, a wrong price. Do not trust a link the model gives you until you open it. also: ойдан шығарылған жауап training → оқыту The process of showing a model enormous amounts of text and adjusting the billions of numbers inside it. fine-tuning → қосымша оқыту Training a ready model further on your own examples so it fits one narrow job. To add facts use RAG, not fine-tuning. also: бейімдеу dataset → деректер жиынтығы A collection of examples gathered to train or to test a model. also: деректер жинағы avoid: датасет parameters → параметрлер The numbers inside a model that get adjusted during training; the count is how model sizes are compared. weights → салмақтар The trained values a model stores; everything it seems to know lives in them. neural network → нейрондық желі A structure of simple calculations stacked in layers that learns from examples instead of fixed rules. also: нейрожелі avoid: нейросеть machine learning → машиналық оқыту Getting a computer to find the rule from

docs.title: The words
docs.section: AI basics
docs.text: examples instead of you writing the rule by hand. deep learning → терең оқыту Machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers; it is what made modern AI possible. embedding → эмбеддинг Turning a piece of text into a list of numbers so that texts with similar meaning end up close together. Embeddings let search find the meaning, not just the exact word. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) → RAG stays in Latin First finding the relevant passages in your own documents, then pasting them into the prompt so the model answers from them. With RAG the model answers from your documents and can point at the source. inference → инференс The moment a trained model actually answers your request; this is what you pay for. also: жауап шығару reasoning model → пайымдайтын модель A model that spends extra tokens thinking a problem through before answering: stronger, but slower and dearer. Give a tricky bug to a reasoning model and a rename to a fast one. extended thinking → кеңейтілген ойлану режимі A mode that lets the model use more tokens on thinking before it writes the answer. mult

docs.title: The words
docs.section: AI basics
docs.text: imodal → мультимодальды Able to understand more than text: images, audio or video as well. Show a multimodal model a screenshot of a design and ask for the page. benchmark → бенчмарк A fixed set of tasks used to compare models with each other. A benchmark score is a hint, not a promise about your own task. generative AI → генеративті ЖИ AI that produces new text, code, images or sound instead of picking from ready answers. open-weight model → ашық салмақты модель A model whose weights anyone can download and run on their own machine. local LLM → жергілікті LLM A model that runs on your own laptop with no internet: free and private, but weaker than a hosted frontier model. With Ollama your prompts never leave the computer. quantization → квантизация Shrinking a model by storing its numbers with less precision, so it fits on ordinary hardware. A 4-bit model needs roughly 0.6-0.7 GB of memory per billion parameters. natural language processing (NLP) → табиғи тілді өңдеу The field that teaches computers to read and write human language. chatbot → чат-бот A program you talk to in question

docs.title: The words
docs.section: AI basics
docs.text: -and-answer form. rate limit → сұрау шегі The maximum number of requests you may send in a given period. function calling → функция шақыру The mechanism that lets a model reply with «run this function with these values» instead of replying with text. Function calling is what turns a plain chat model into an agent. pre-training → алдын ала оқыту The first and longest stage of training, where the model reads an enormous slice of the internet and learns language itself. knowledge cutoff → білім шегі The date after which the model has read nothing, so newer libraries and events simply do not exist for it. If the library is newer than the cutoff, paste its documentation into the prompt yourself. also: оқыту деректерінің соңғы күні frontier model → алдыңғы қатарлы модель The strongest model a company currently offers, usually also the slowest and the most expensive. Today four or five labs have a frontier model, and they change places every few months. closed model → жабық модель A model whose weights stay private, so the only way to use it is through the company that made it. A closed mod

docs.title: The words
docs.section: AI basics
docs.text: el is usually stronger; an open-weight one is usually more private. also: жабық салмақты модель model provider → модель жеткізуші The company whose servers actually run the model you are talking to: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Mistral and others. Most tools let you change provider without rewriting a single prompt. also: провайдер transformer → трансформер The internal design shared by almost every modern language model, which lets it weigh each word against all the others. prompt caching → промптты кэштеу Storing the unchanged beginning of a prompt so that repeat requests come back cheaper and faster. Put the long standing instructions at the top, where they can be cached. streaming → ағынмен беру Showing the answer token by token while it is still being written, instead of waiting for all of it. avoid: стриминг input and output tokens → кіріс және шығыс токендері What you send counts as input tokens and what the model writes counts as output tokens, and output usually costs several times more. A long file you paste in is charged as input tokens on every single turn. evaluation (eval

docs.title: The words
docs.section: AI basics
docs.text: ) → бағалау A repeatable test you run against a model or a prompt to see whether a change really helped. Without evals you are only guessing that the new prompt is better. also: eval non-determinism → нәтиженің тұрақсыздығы The same prompt can give a different answer each time, because the model picks its tokens with a little randomness. It worked once, so run it again before you decide it is fixed. AI assistant → ЖИ-көмекші A chat-shaped AI that answers and drafts for you but does nothing on your computer by itself. An assistant suggests, an agent goes and does it. also: ассистент avoid: ИИ-ассистент AI literacy → ЖИ сауаттылығы Knowing what these tools can and cannot do, and checking what they produce instead of trusting it. AI literacy is now as basic a skill as using a search engine. bias → бейімділік A lopsided pattern a model picked up from its training data and quietly repeats in its answers. A model has read far more English than Kazakh, and that shows. also: жүйелі ауытқу AI safety → ЖИ қауіпсіздігі The work of making a model refuse harmful requests and behave predictably on

docs.title: The words
docs.section: AI basics
docs.text: ce it is given real power. GPU → GPU stays in Latin The chip that does the heavy parallel arithmetic behind training and running models. A local model runs on your GPU; a hosted one runs on someone else’s. also: графикалық процессор avoid: видеокарта speech to text → дауысты мәтінге айналдыру Turning what you say out loud into text the model can read. Dictating a long prompt is usually faster than typing it. image model → сурет жасайтын модель A model that produces pictures from a written description instead of producing text. Use an image model for the logo and a language model for the code. AI coding tool → ЖИ-кодтау құралы Any editor or terminal program with a model built into it: Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Gemini CLI, Codex. They all work the same way, so learn one properly and you can switch to any other. Claude → Claude stays in Latin Anthropic's family of models, and the assistant this course leans on most. Show the error text to Claude and ask why it happens. ChatGPT → ChatGPT stays in Latin OpenAI's assistant, the one most people meet first. It is worth c

docs.title: The words
docs.section: AI basics
docs.text: omparing ChatGPT's answer with Claude's on the same question. Gemini → Gemini stays in Latin Google's family of models, strong on long documents and on images. A name whose reading is unclear takes a descriptor noun, not a hyphenated ending. RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) → адам пікірі арқылы оқыту A later training stage where people rate the model's answers, so it learns which kind of reply is actually useful. also: RLHF token price → токен бағасы What you pay per million tokens, counted separately for what you send in and what the model writes back. A Kazakh prompt costs more, because the same meaning takes more tokens. GPU (graphics processing unit) → графикалық процессор (GPU) The chip that does the enormous number of calculations a model needs; it is the reason AI costs money. A local model runs on your own GPU; a hosted one runs in a data centre. also: GPU avoid: видеокарта

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Agents and agentic coding
docs.text: AI agent → ЖИ-агент A model running in a loop: it takes a goal, calls tools itself, looks at the result and tries again. The agent reads the file, edits it, runs the tests, sees the error and fixes it. also: агент avoid: ИИ-агент agent loop → агент циклі Look at the goal, choose an action, observe the result, repeat until it is done or it needs you. The power of the loop is feedback: the agent sees real results instead of guessing. agentic coding → агенттік кодтау Writing software by directing an agent instead of typing most of the code yourself. agentic engineering → агенттік инженерия The professional version of vibe coding: the agent writes, but tests, review and git stay in place. The step from vibe coding to agentic engineering starts with one test. tool use → құрал қолдану Giving a model the ability to act: read a file, run a command, call an API. Without tools a model can only produce text. tool call → құрал шақыру The structured request a model makes, such as read this file, which your program then executes. MCP (Model Context Protocol) → MCP stays in Latin An open standard f

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Agents and agentic coding
docs.text: or plugging external tools and data into AI apps, so one server works in many of them. MCP is USB-C for AI: one connector instead of a separate cable for every pair. MCP server → MCP сервері stays in Latin A small program that exposes the tools and data of one system, such as GitHub, Figma or your database. Install only servers you trust: a tool description is untrusted input too. subagent → субагент A helper agent the main one starts: it works in its own context window and returns a short summary. Give a long investigation to a subagent so your main window stays clean. also: қосалқы агент skill (Agent Skills) → skill stays in Latin A folder that describes how to do one job properly, which the agent opens only when that job comes up. A skill beats stuffing everything into CLAUDE.md: it enters the context only when needed. also: дағды hook → hook stays in Latin Your own script that runs automatically at a fixed point in the agent run, for example a linter after every edit. A rule that must never be broken belongs in a hook, not in CLAUDE.md. CLAUDE.md → CLAUDE.md файлы stays in Latin

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Agents and agentic coding
docs.text: The project memory loaded at the start of every session: commands, rules and quirks the agent cannot guess. Keep it under 200 lines: every line costs context in every session. AGENTS.md → AGENTS.md файлы stays in Latin The same idea as CLAUDE.md but in a shared format that many different tools read. One AGENTS.md is read by Claude Code, Codex and Cursor alike. plan mode → жоспарлау режимі A mode where the agent reads and explores but does not touch the code, and writes out what it intends to do. Review the 200-line plan, not the 2000-line diff. permission mode → рұқсат режимі The setting that decides which actions the agent may take without asking you first. auto mode → авто режим A mode where a separate checking model reviews the actions instead of asking you about each one. Auto mode is a seatbelt, not an isolated sandbox. session → сеанс One continuous conversation with the agent; when it ends, its context is gone. After two failed corrections, clear the session and write a better first prompt. memory (agent) → жад Notes and files the agent keeps between sessions, because the conv

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Agents and agentic coding
docs.text: ersation itself does not survive. compaction → қысу Turning a long conversation into a short summary so work can continue in a fresh window. For an unrelated task clearing is better than compacting, and it is free. also: compaction context engineering → контекст инженериясы The craft of giving the model exactly the tokens it needs at each step, and nothing more. Context engineering is what prompt engineering became once agents started running in loops. checkpoint → бақылау нүктесі A snapshot the tool takes before an edit, so you can step back to it. A checkpoint is local undo, git is permanent undo. worktree → worktree stays in Latin A separate folder with its own branch that shares one repository history, so parallel sessions never collide. Give parallel agents a worktree each, so they do not fight over the same file. also: бөлек жұмыс қалтасы multi-agent system → көпагенттік жүйе Several agents splitting one task between them. It typically costs three to ten times the tokens, so try one agent first. orchestrator → жетекші агент The agent that splits the work, hands parts to worker

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Agents and agentic coding
docs.text: agents and collects the results. also: orchestrator evaluator agent → бағалаушы агент An agent whose only job is to check the finished work against the agreed criteria. Separate the maker from the checker: an agent grades its own work far too generously. eval → eval stays in Latin A test suite for the agent and your own instructions: a set of real tasks you rerun after every change. The minimal version: keep 10-20 tasks that once went wrong and rerun them. also: бағалау жиынтығы verification loop → тексеру циклі Anything that gives the agent a pass or fail signal it can read itself: a test, a build, a screenshot. If you cannot verify it, do not ship it. guardrails → қорғаныс шектері The limits that keep an agent from going too far: permissions, tests, folders it may not touch. human in the loop → адам бақылауы Keeping a person in the chain so that important actions are seen and approved before they happen. harness → harness stays in Latin The scaffolding around a long-running agent: a progress file, a feature list and a fixed ritual for each session. also: агент ортасы agent loop scr

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Agents and agentic coding
docs.text: ipt (Ralph loop) → Ralph циклі stays in Latin A simple shell loop that feeds the same prompt to the agent again and again, each time in a fresh context. If you start a loop, always cap the number of iterations. slash command → «/» пәрмені A ready-made action inside the agent, typed with a slash at the start. also: slash command avoid: слэш-команда cloud agent → бұлттық агент An agent running on a machine in the cloud rather than on your laptop, which you watch from a browser or phone. agent team → агенттер тобы A lead agent and several teammates sharing one task list and messaging each other. If you run a team, give every file exactly one owner. spec-driven development → спецификацияға негізделген әзірлеу Writing what and why first, then how, then the task list, and only then letting the agent code against those files. headless mode → headless режимі stays in Latin Running the agent from a single command with no interactive screen, which is what scripts and automation need. token budget → токен бюджеті How many tokens you are willing to spend on one task; set it before you start anyt

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Agents and agentic coding
docs.text: hing that runs on its own. model routing → модельді таңдап бағыттау Sending each kind of work to the model that suits it: a cheap one for simple steps, a strong one for architecture. agent → агент An AI that does not just answer but works in a loop: it decides, uses tools, checks the result and keeps going until the task is done. Tell an agent the goal, not which keys to press. also: ЖИ-агент avoid: ИИ-агент coding agent → кодтау агенті An agent that can read your project, write files, run commands and see the errors it has just caused. Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor and Copilot are all coding agents, so try more than one. tool → құрал Anything an agent is allowed to call: reading a file, running a command, searching the web, asking a database. avoid: инструмент skill → skill stays in Latin A folder of instructions and files an agent loads only when a task needs them, which keeps the context small. Put the deploy steps your team repeats into a skill instead of into every prompt. also: дағды auto-accept → автоматты мақұлдау Letting the agent apply its changes without asking yo

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Agents and agentic coding
docs.text: u each time, which is fast and is also how people lose work. Do not switch auto-accept on before the work is committed. background agent → фондық агент An agent that keeps working on its own while you do something else and reports back when it is finished. Send the boring cleanup to a background agent and carry on with the feature. agent instructions file (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) → агент нұсқаулары файлы A file at the root of the project that every agent reads first: how to run the code, what the rules are, what it must never touch. Write CLAUDE.md in English and keep it short, because every session pays for it in tokens. autonomy → дербестік How far an agent may go on its own before it has to come back and ask you. Raise autonomy only where a mistake is cheap to undo. also: автономдық guardrail → қорғаныс шегі A rule set in advance that stops an agent doing damage even when its reasoning goes wrong. Never handing the agent production credentials is exactly such a guardrail. also: шектеу AI editor → ЖИ редакторы A code editor with an agent built in, such as Cursor, Windsurf or VS Code

docs.title: The words
docs.section: Agents and agentic coding
docs.text: with Copilot, which sees your open files and edits them in place. You get an approval box, because this is a Bash command. The deny rule never fired. Approve, and the fake key is on your screen. Bash rules match the text of the command , not the program that runs. Bash(rm *) does not stop /bin/rm or bash -c 'rm ...' , and a Read deny does not stop a script that opens the file itself. These rules are convenience, not a security boundary. ! docs.text: ✦ The four rules that break skills name is lowercase-with-hyphens, at most 64 characters, and matches the folder name. description says what it does and when to use it — that sentence is how the agent decides to load it. Anthropic’s January 2026 guidance puts a multi-agent setup at three to ten times the tokens of one agent for the same task, and says to try single-agent options first. Its earlier research system measured about fifteen times the tokens of chat ; coding has fewer parallel parts than research. 3–10x tokens of one agent, same task Anthropic, 23 Jan 2026 ↗ 16 parallel Claudes that built a C compiler Anthropic, 5 Feb 2026 ↗ ~$20,000 API cost of that two-week run Anthropic, 5 Feb 2026 ↗ That C compiler is the ceiling: sixteen instances, roughly 2,000 sessions, about 100,000 lines of Rust. It worked because the test suite was near-perfect. Without an automated check, parallel agents just multiply unverified code. Anything sequential. docs.text: Pre-flight 0 / 6 done ✓ git status is clean in the main folder ✓ Your latest work is pushed — worktrees branch from the remote default branch, not your local HEAD ✓ .gitignore contains the line .claude/worktrees/ ✓ You have run plain claude in this folder before, so the workspace is trusted ✓ CLAUDE.md exists and says something useful about this project ✓ You have opened /usage today and know where your limits are ! The pushed-work trap By default --worktree branches from the remote default branch, not from what you have locally. Commit without pushing and both agents start from old code. Push first; the Deeper box has the alternative.

docs.section: Everything you pay for is counted in tokens
docs.text: A token is what the model actually reads and writes: a common word, a word fragment, or a punctuation mark. A token is what the model actually reads and writes: a common word, a word fragment, or a punctuation mark. Every price, every limit and every “too long” error is counted in tokens, never in characters or words. The vocabulary is fixed and learned during training: frequent strings become one token, rare ones get chopped into many. Think LEGO — some text snaps together from big pre-moulded pieces, the rest is built out of 1x1 bricks. English runs about 1.2 to 1.8 tokens per word. Claude’s newer tokenizer produces about 30% more tokens for the same text than the old one, so 1M tokens is now around 555,000 words, not the 750,000 the old rule promised ( Anthropic model overview ). Token counter 22 tokens Models do not read letters or words. They read tokens. Type anything and watch how it gets chopped up. docs.text: on and save it to the dat abas e. 22 tokens 71 characters 13 words 3.2 chars / token Cost for 1,000 messages this size $ 0.07 at $3 per million input tokens ⓘ This is a close approximation of how a BPE tokenizer splits text, not the exact tokenizer of any one model. The pattern it shows is real: Latin text packs ~4 characters into a token, Cyrillic text often gets 1–2, so the same sentence in Kazakh can cost 2–3× more. Why you care Your context window, your bill and your speed are all measured in tokens. The same meaning written in Kazakh costs more than in English — so for long agent instructions, English is usually the cheaper language, even when you talk to the user in Kazakh.

docs.section: Kazakh costs several times more than English
docs.text: In the Sherkala paper’s Table 1, the Llama-3.1 tokenizer needs 4.73 tokens per Kazakh word, against 2.56 for… In the Sherkala paper’s Table 1, the Llama-3.1 tokenizer needs 4.73 tokens per Kazakh word , against 2.56 for Russian and 2.23 for Turkish. Adding Kazakh tokens to the vocabulary cut that to 2.04 ( arXiv ). A 2026 measurement puts English at 1.23 tokens per word across six public tokenizers ( arXiv ). Across 17 tokenizers, the gap between the cheapest and the most expensive language reaches 15x ( Petrov et al., NeurIPS 2023 ). 4.73 tokens per Kazakh word, Llama-3.1 tokenizer Sherkala, Table 1 ↗ 1.23 tokens per English word, mean of six tokenizers Tokenizer Tax, 2026 ↗ 15x largest gap between languages, 17 tokenizers Petrov et al., NeurIPS 2023 ↗ Three reasons stack up. Cyrillic letters take two bytes each in UTF-8. The Kazakh-specific letters (ә ғ қ ң ө ұ ү һ і) are rare in training data. And Kazakh is agglutinative: one word like “үйлеріміздегілерге” carries a whole English phrase. The working rule: Kazakh costs about 2x English on the best modern tokenizers, and 3.5 to 4.7x

docs.text: The context window is everything the model can see at once: your instructions, the conversation so far, every… The context window is everything the model can see at once: your instructions, the conversation so far, every file it read, every tool result, the reply it is writing. Anything outside it does not exist — no memory of your last session unless something puts it back. Only the papers lying on the desk can be used; when it overflows, something gets filed away. 1M tokens is the normal ceiling: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and DeepSeek all reach it. Mistral stops at 256k and Claude Haiku 4.5 at 200k. Fill the context window 16.9 k / 200k An agent has one desk, and everything it knows about your task has to fit on it. docs.section: Temperature decides how surprising the next word can be
docs.text: Temperature is the randomness dial for picking each next token. Temperature is the randomness dial for picking each next token. Near 0 the model almost always takes the most likely option: repeatable and dull. Turn it up and less likely options get through — more variety, more risk. A chef at 0 follows the recipe; higher up, they improvise. Low for code and data extraction, higher for brainstorming names. Some reasoning models set this themselves and ignore what you ask for.

docs.section: Hallucination is the normal failure mode
docs.text: A hallucination is output that sounds right and is invented: a library function that does not exist, a… A hallucination is output that sounds right and is invented: a library function that does not exist, a citation with a real-looking author, a wrong price stated confidently. The model generates plausible text instead of checking a source, and almost never signals doubt. Picture a student who did not study and still writes a fluent, confident exam answer. Two defences. Grounding: give it the docs, let it search, let it run the code. Verification: tests, links, your own eyes ( module 10 ). Anthropic says the same — ask for evidence, not assertions ( best practices ). ❯ Grounding prompt any agent · paste before your question Copy Before you answer, follow these rules: 1. List the files you actually opened, with line ranges. Do not answer from memory. 2. Answer only from what you read. If the answer is not in the repo, say "not in the repo" instead of guessing. 3. For every claim about how the code behaves, give me the command you ran and its real output. Evidence, not assertions. 4. I

docs.section: Tools let a model touch the real world
docs.text: A model can only produce text. Tool use (also called function calling) means you describe functions it may… A model can only produce text. Tool use (also called function calling) means you describe functions it may call — read a file, run a command, query an API — and it replies with a structured request instead of prose. Your program runs it and hands the result back. A head chef who never touches the stove: precise orders out, tasted results back in.

docs.title: AI in Plain Language
docs.section: An agent is a model running in a loop
docs.text: An agent is the model plus tools plus a loop: read the goal and the state, choose an action, observe the… An agent is the model plus tools plus a loop: read the goal and the state, choose an action, observe the result, repeat until done or until it needs you. Claude Code is exactly this — read files, edit, run the tests, read the error, fix, run again. The power is feedback: the model reacts to real results instead of guessing. The risk is that errors compound, which is why permission prompts ( module 07 ) and git commits ( module 09 ) exist. A mechanic, not an oracle: try something, listen to the engine, adjust.

docs.section: RAG is an open-book exam
docs.text: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means searching your own documents for relevant passages, then pasting… RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means searching your own documents for relevant passages, then pasting them into the prompt. The model answers from them: fresh or private knowledge without retraining, and it can point at where the answer came from. The quality is all in the search step. Retrieve the wrong passage and you get a fluent wrong answer with a citation attached. Same student, same brain — but now the right page is open.

docs.section: MCP is one connector instead of ten
docs.text: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for plugging external tools and data into AI apps. The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for plugging external tools and data into AI apps. One server for GitHub, Figma or your database works in Claude Code, in Cursor and elsewhere, with no rewriting. It exposes tools (actions), resources (data) and prompts (templates); the AI app is the client. Think USB-C: one connector instead of a cable for every pair of devices. It started at Anthropic in November 2024, was adopted by OpenAI and Google DeepMind during 2025, and was donated in December 2025 to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. The current spec version is 2026-07-28 , which made the protocol stateless and deprecated the old HTTP+SSE transport ( MCP specification ). ! Treat every MCP server as untrusted code Tool descriptions and tool results are input your model acts on, and the spec itself calls tools “arbitrary code execution”. Install servers only from vendors you trust, and read the permissions they ask for ( module 11 ). The official directory is the

docs.section: Reasoning models think on scratch paper first
docs.text: A reasoning model spends extra tokens working through a problem — planning, trying an approach, checking… A reasoning model spends extra tokens working through a problem — planning, trying an approach, checking itself — before it writes the answer you see. Stronger at maths, debugging and multi-step planning. Slower and more expensive, because thinking tokens are billed as output. In 2026 this is a dial, not a separate product: Claude’s adaptive thinking with an effort setting, GPT’s reasoning levels, Gemini’s thinking budget. In Claude Code the dial is /effort : low , medium , high (the default on most models), xhigh and max ( model config docs ). Go deeper Why your effort setting shows up on the bill Thinking tokens are charged at the output rate, and output costs four to six times input almost everywhere. An agent also re-sends its whole conversation on every turn, so a long session is dominated by re-read input — cached, but still billed. That is why /clear is a cost lever, not just hygiene; lowering effort on simple tasks is the second ( Claude Code costs ).

docs.text: In September 2025 Anthropic named the discipline. In September 2025 Anthropic named the discipline. Context engineering is choosing which tokens occupy the window when the model answers. The window is finite ( module 02 ), and recall drops as it fills — the effect the post calls context rot. ( Effective context engineering for AI agents ) So your memory file is not a folder of documentation. It is a standing charge, paid again in every session — including the ones about a file it has nothing to do with. The post also sets the target for how a standing rule should read: the “right altitude”. Specific enough to steer the model, general enough to work as a heuristic. Not brittle if-else rules. docs.text: AGENTS.md is the open-standard version of the same idea: plain Markdown, no required fields, a predictable… AGENTS.md is the open-standard version of the same idea: plain Markdown, no required fields, a predictable place for commands, style, security notes and PR rules. Its site calls it a “README for agents”. ( agents.md ) It is no longer one company’s format. On 9 December 2025 the Linux Foundation announced the Agentic AI Foundation, with three founding projects: MCP from Anthropic, goose from Block, and AGENTS.md from OpenAI. Platinum members include AWS, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI. Today the file is read by Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Aider, Zed, VS Code, JetBrains Junie, Jules, Warp, Devin and more. Claude Code reads it too, with one rule. Since v2.1.277 it reads AGENTS.md natively when there is no CLAUDE.md in or above the working directory. docs.text: Static means the site is built once into a folder of plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and that folder is… Static means the site is built once into a folder of plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and that folder is copied to machines around the world. Nothing runs per visitor, which makes it the cheapest, fastest and hardest to break. This site is static: npm run build turns the source into dist/ , and dist/ is the website. Server-rendered means a program runs for each request: it checks who you are, reads the database, calls a paid API. That code runs out of the visitor’s sight, the only place a secret can live. Two shapes: one long-running server, or small serverless functions (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Functions) that wake per request and sleep again. Keep as much static as you can; push the dynamic part into the smallest possible function. A static page costs you nothing. A function spends budget every time someone loads it — Cloudflare’s free Workers tier allows 100,000 requests a day and 10 ms of CPU per invocation, while Pages lists no bandwidth cap at all for static assets. docs.text: Your site has an address the moment it deploys — something like qairu-event.pages.dev. Your site has an address the moment it deploys — something like qairu-event.pages.dev . A custom domain is a nicer name pointed at the same place. DNS translates a name into the address of the machine that answers for it. Attaching a domain means adding a record — usually a CNAME : “this name means that server”. Your host then issues the SSL certificate that turns http:// into https:// , free and automatic. docs.text: Five commands cover most days. Word What it is Repo Your project folder plus its full history, in a hidden .git folder. Offline, no account needed. Commit One snapshot: the state of every file, plus a message explaining the change. Branch A parallel line of work. main stays untouched until you merge. Remote A copy of the repo on a server, usually GitHub. You push to it, you pull from it. Pull request A proposal to merge one branch into another. Shows which lines changed and runs checks first. Five commands cover most days. bash Copy cd qairu-signup git init git status git add . git commit -m "chore: first working version" git log --oneline git status is the one you run most: what changed since the last snapshot, and what goes into the next. git add stages files, git commit takes the snapshot, git log --oneline reads the history back.

docs.text: A .gitignore file tells git which paths to pretend it cannot see. A .gitignore file tells git which paths to pretend it cannot see. Four lines cover a typical project: .gitignore Copy .env node_modules/ dist/ .claude/worktrees/ .env holds your API keys ( module 08 ) and must never be committed. node_modules/ is reinstallable and enormous, dist/ is generated, .claude/worktrees/ holds Claude Code’s parallel working copies. ✕ A committed secret does not get uncommitted Deleting a key from a file and committing again does not remove it. Every earlier snapshot still holds it, and if you pushed, so does someone else’s server. Treat any key that reached a commit as public: issue a new one, revoke the old. docs.section: Write commit messages you can still read at 2 a.m.
docs.text: A commit message has one job: let a future reader decide in two seconds whether this is the commit to undo. A commit message has one job: let a future reader decide in two seconds whether this is the commit to undo. Conventional commits give it a shape — a type, an optional scope, one line of description. git log --oneline feat(signup): store reservations in D1 fix(form): reject an empty email instead of saving it test(form): cover the duplicate-email case refactor(api): split the handler into two files docs(readme): how to run the dev server chore(deps): bump astro Six types carry almost everything: feat , fix , docs , refactor , test , chore . Keep the first line short enough to scan, and put the why in the body. Then git log --oneline is a changelog you can revert line by line. Anthropic’s write-up on harnesses for long-running agents gives the agent the same habit: commit after each unit of progress, so a later session can find its way back to a state that worked.

docs.text: Claude Code has its own safety net: every prompt creates a checkpoint, and files are snapshotted before each… Claude Code has its own safety net: every prompt creates a checkpoint, and files are snapshotted before each edit. Esc Esc on an empty input, or /rewind , restores code, conversation, or just one of them. For “that last edit was wrong” it beats any git command. The checkpointing docs say checkpoints are not a replacement for git. Only the 100 most recent per session are kept, and they are swept about 30 days after the session last saved one. They do not track changes from Bash commands such as rm , mv and cp , most subagent edits, edits made outside the session, or symlinked and hard-linked files. ! The failure case is exactly the uncovered one The run that hurts is the one where the agent shells out — moves a folder, deletes a directory, regenerates files with a script. Checkpoints do not cover that. A commit does, because it does not care who changed the file or how.

You will also get a login form nobody asked for, a phone-number field you did not want, an invented event with an invented date, and a save button that writes to a variable which disappears when the tab closes. None of that is a malfunction. Each one is a decision you did not make, so the model made it for you. Module 03 gave you the habit: decide before you prompt. This module gives you the file. A decision in your head is one the agent cannot read. One you typed into a chat three sessions ago is gone. One page, on disk, at the start of every build. Four hundred lines and a rendered page in ninety seconds. Impressive on the projector. You have no idea what it decided, and finding out means reading all four hundred. Three questions you answer in half a minute, then about twenty lines of plan. You review the plan instead of the diff. The right-hand column does not need a bigger model. It needs a page that existed before the session started.

docs.section: Five questions that fit on one page
docs.text: PRD stands for product requirements document. PRD stands for product requirements document. Ignore the corporate name. Here it is one page, five answers, written before anything exists and saved as PRD.md next to your code. Some tools call the same file SPEC.md . Pick one name and use it everywhere. Problem. One sentence about the pain, not the feature. “Seats fill up in a Telegram thread and nobody knows who is actually coming” is a problem. “We need a sign-up form” is a solution that smuggles in decisions you have not examined. User. Specific enough to picture one person. A student in Astana, on a phone, on mobile data, deciding right now whether she has a seat. Her constraints — small screen, slow connection, no patience — are requirements in disguise. The one job. People do not want your product. They hire it to get a job done, and fire it when something does that job faster. Your user is not hiring a sign-up page. She is hiring certainty that she has a seat. Write that job as one sentence in her words. If it contains “and”, you have two jobs: keep the one that hurts more. Defini

docs.section: The not-building list is the part that pays
docs.text: Every line in it is a decision the agent no longer gets to make for you. Every line in it is a decision the agent no longer gets to make for you. It is also the only part of a PRD that gets shorter as you improve. A first build you can finish in one sitting: one page, no login, no payments, no admin panel, data in the browser or one file, deployed by dragging a folder. Everything else is version two. If the plan comes back bigger than you expected, cut the must-have list in half and ask again. ! Some things are out of scope for a different reason Do not let an agent invent your login, your database permissions or your payment flow while you are learning. A scan of 1,645 Lovable-built apps found 170 that let anyone read user names, email addresses, financial information and secret API keys ( Semafor, 29 May 2025 ). When you genuinely need accounts, use a managed service and have a human read that part ( module 11 ). For a first build, “no accounts” is a security decision, not a limitation. docs.text: Weak. The sign-up should feel fast and look clean. An agent will cheerfully claim both, and you have nothing… Weak. The sign-up should feel fast and look clean. An agent will cheerfully claim both, and you have nothing to argue with. Strong. docs.section: Hand it over: read, ask, plan, do not code
docs.text: Three questions, not “any questions”. ❯ Hand the PRD to the agent Claude Code · plan mode Copy Read PRD.md. Do not write any code yet. 1. Tell me back, in five lines, what you understood: the problem, the user, the one job, my definition of done, and what is out of scope. 2. Ask me exactly 3 questions — the three points in the PRD where guessing wrong would cost the most. One at a time. 3. After I answer, write PLAN.md: - ordered steps, each small enough to verify on its own - the files each step creates or changes - the check that proves that step works - what you will NOT touch - any assumption you are making that I should confirm Stop there and wait for my approval. If a step turns out to be wrong while you are implementing it, stop and update the plan instead of improvising. Three questions, not “any questions”. A hard limit forces the agent to rank, and the three it picks show you which parts of your page are thin. You run this prompt for real in module 07 .

docs.section: Spec-driven development is a dial, not a religion
docs.text: Turn this one page into a whole toolchain and you have spec-driven development. Turn this one page into a whole toolchain and you have spec-driven development. GitHub’s Spec Kit is the best-known version: open source under MIT, Python 3.11 or newer, installed with uv tool install specify-cli and started with specify init my-project --integration copilot . Its commands run in order: /speckit-constitution for project principles, /speckit-specify for what and why, /speckit-plan for the technical approach, /speckit-tasks for work items, /speckit-implement to build, /speckit-converge to re-check progress against the spec. Implement and converge repeat until it reports that it has converged ( github.com/github/spec-kit ). It moves fast: seven releases landed between 1 and 21 September 2026. Read the README, not last year’s tutorial. You do not need any of it today. Testing these toolkits, Birgitta Böckeler found the elaborate process created a false sense of control: the agent still skipped some instructions and over-applied others ( martinfowler.com, 15 Oct 2025 ). More markdown is not mo

docs.section: Spec-driven development is a dial, not a religion
docs.text: re certainty. One page you reread beats six templates you skimmed. Go deeper Three different things people mean by 'spec-driven' Böckeler separates them. Spec-first : you write the spec, the agent builds, and afterwards the code is the truth. Spec-anchored : the spec stays alive, and every change goes through it before it reaches the code. Spec-as-source : humans edit only the spec, and the generated code is marked do-not-edit. All three get called the same name, which is why people argue past each other. Two other toolkits, for when you go looking: AWS Kiro splits a spec into requirements.md , design.md and tasks.md with approval gates between the phases ( kiro.dev/docs/specs ); BMAD now ships as skills and plugins around a Clarify → Plan → Build and verify → Learn and adjust loop ( github.com/bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD ). docs.section: Every command happens somewhere
docs.text: A terminal always stands inside one folder — the current directory — and most commands act on it. A terminal always stands inside one folder — the current directory — and most commands act on it. Beginner confusion (“the command did nothing”, “file not found”) is usually “I was standing in the wrong place”. A path is the address of a folder or file. / separates the parts on macOS, Linux, WSL and Git Bash; \ on native Windows. The Claude Code binary lands at ~/.local/bin/claude on macOS and Linux, at %USERPROFILE%\.local\bin\claude.exe on Windows ( setup docs ). ~ means your home folder. . means here. .. means one level up. One rule: always cd into your project folder before starting an agent. Start it on the Desktop instead and every other project you own sits inside its working directory. One project, one folder, one session.

docs.section: node_modules is not your code
docs.text: A package manager downloads the libraries your project needs, plus the libraries those need, and records the… A package manager downloads the libraries your project needs, plus the libraries those need, and records the exact versions in a lock file so every machine installs the same thing. For JavaScript that is npm, pnpm or bun; for Python, pip or uv. package.json — what you asked for: the dependencies and the named commands ( dev , build , test ). the lock file — what you actually got, down to the exact version. node_modules/ — the downloaded code itself. Hundreds of folders. Nobody reads it. npm install — the command that turns the first two into the third. node_modules never goes into git: it is enormous, and one command rebuilds it anywhere. A Claude Code git worktree is a fresh checkout with no node_modules , so you reinstall it ( worktrees ). If an agent proposes committing that folder, say no.

docs.text: Environment variables are named values that live outside your code and reach the program when it starts: API… Environment variables are named values that live outside your code and reach the program when it starts: API keys, a database address, NODE_ENV=production . They keep secrets out of the repository, and let the same code behave differently on your laptop and on the server. Locally they sit in a .env file listed in .gitignore . On a host you paste them into the dashboard. One correct order, no exceptions: Build the app. Get it working. Run git init , commit everything, push to GitHub. Add .gitignore later, when a tutorial mentions it. The key is now in the repository history. Deleting the file does not remove it. The only fix is to revoke that key and issue a new one. Create .gitignore with .env and node_modules/ in it before the first commit . Commit a .env.example with the key names and empty values. docs.text: device, and anyone can read it in the browser developer tools. They belong on the backend or in the host’s dashboard ( module 11 ). Go deeper Can I just tell my agent not to read .env? You can, and you should — but it is not a lock. In .claude/settings.json a rule like "deny": ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)", "Read(./secrets/**)"] blocks the Read tool, plus cat , head , tail and sed in Bash. It does not stop a script that opens the file itself: Bash rules match command text, not the program. The permissions docs are plain about it — convenience, not a security boundary. Real isolation comes from sandboxing, which native Windows does not support. Rotate any key that has ever been committed or pasted into a chat.

docs.section: “It works on my machine” is a diagnosis, not a joke
docs.text: It means your machine has something the other machine does not. It means your machine has something the other machine does not. Five usual candidates, all checkable in two minutes. A missing environment variable. Your .env exists locally and nowhere else. Fix: add the variables in the host dashboard. An uncommitted file. It works because the file is on your disk, not in the project. Fix: git status . Dependencies never installed. The other machine has package.json but no node_modules . Fix: run the install command. Capital letters. Windows treats Hero.astro and hero.astro as the same file. Most deploy servers run Linux and treat them as two, so an import that works locally fails in the build. Fix: match the filename character for character. A different version. A newer or older runtime than yours. Claude Code shows the pattern: the npm install route needs Node.js 22 or newer ( setup docs ). Working on your machine is not done. Deployed is done ( module 12 ).

docs.section: Four streams, four questions
docs.text: People say “check the logs” as if there were one thing. People say “check the logs” as if there were one thing. There are four. Stream The question it answers Where it lives Logs What happened, in order, at what time? Your host’s dashboard, by default Errors What broke, how often, for how many people? An error tracker you wire up yourself Traces Which step inside one request was slow? A tracing backend, usually the same tool Analytics What did people actually do — and give up on? An analytics tool you add to the page Logs are free and already on; the rest you add when the project has real users.

Time, route, status code, request id. 500 means your server broke, not the user. Keep that request id — it finds every other log line from the same visit. The second line is the actual bug. TypeError is the kind; the words after the colon are the sentence that matters. Something was undefined and the code called .trim() on it anyway. The lines below are the call chain, newest first. Skip every frame inside node_modules or the platform’s own runtime. The first frame in a file you wrote is where you look: src/lib/signup.js , line 42. docs.text: Your host’s log stream is a firehose that forgets. Your host’s log stream is a firehose that forgets. An error tracker is the opposite: your app reports each crash, and it keeps the trace, groups duplicates, counts how many people hit each one, and pings you when a new one appears. Sentry is one such tool; PostHog does the same job for the analytics row above. Both have a free tier; check the current limits on their own pricing pages, not on this one. The vendor matters less than the rule: the error must land somewhere that keeps it and can interrupt you. ✦ Before you wire a dashboard into your agent Claude Code reaches an outside service two ways: an MCP server, or that service’s own command-line tool. docs.section: Measure four numbers, not forty
docs.text: Analytics dashboards are built to make you feel something. Analytics dashboards are built to make you feel something. Resist. There is one honest test for any metric: if this number moved tomorrow, what would I do differently? No answer means do not track it. For QAIRU Event Sign-up: how many opened the page, how many started the form, how many finished and got a seat, and how many errors happened in the same window. The gap between the second and third number is your whole product problem, stated as one subtraction. Total visits, likes, “engagement” — those rise whether or not your app works, so they teach nothing. ! Logs are a database you forgot you built Never write an email address, a phone number, an IIN, a password or an API token into a log line or an analytics event. You will paste that log into an agent and a support chat, and log stores are rarely protected the way your database is. Log the request id and the shape of the failure, not the human it happened to.

docs.section: Three reasons to split, and one bad way to split
docs.text: The January 2026 post names three cases where a second agent earns its keep. The January 2026 post names three cases where a second agent earns its keep. Context protection : the side work would flood your main window. Parallelisation : the facets are genuinely independent. Specialisation : a narrow tool set or prompt beats a generalist. A planner plans, a coder codes, a tester tests. Each handoff drops what the previous agent knew but never wrote down. The tester tests what it guessed the feature was. The agent that builds a feature writes its tests too — it already holds the context. Split when the context is separate: a different module, a different file set, a question answerable without the rest.

docs.section: What actually ran that night
docs.text: The point is not that agents can write a website. Three shifts. Research agents wrote long Markdown files. Every claim carried a source URL and a [V] or UNVERIFIED marker. A fact-check agent took the claims most likely to reach a slide — numbers, dates, quotes, prices, commands — opened each primary source and tried to refute them. It caught two of its own team’s errors: a famous five-line agent loop story credits the wrong tool, and a widely repeated rm -rf ~ anecdote paraphrases a GitHub issue that says something else. Both corrections are still in the files, labelled. Only then did content agents write the lessons, using nothing but those files. The point is not that agents can write a website. It is that the run surfaced its own mistakes at 02:00 instead of on stage.

docs.section: Plan mode is the first gate
docs.text: Nothing autonomous starts without a written plan you have read. Nothing autonomous starts without a written plan you have read. Enter plan mode with Shift+Tab , or start with claude --permission-mode plan . Ctrl+G opens the plan in your editor so you can rewrite it before approving. A plan you skimmed is not a plan you read. Make it the default for a repo you run unattended: { "permissions" : { "defaultMode" : "plan" } } The loop is Explore → Plan → Code → Commit ( module 07 ). The docs let you skip the plan when you could describe the diff in one sentence. Never an overnight run.

docs.text: The slow part of building software used to be the code itself. The slow part of building software used to be the code itself. Simon Willison’s guide for coding agents has a chapter titled “writing code is cheap now” ( Agentic Engineering Patterns ). The cost did not disappear. docs.text: The mathematician George Pólya split problem-solving into four steps: understand the problem, devise a plan,… The mathematician George Pólya split problem-solving into four steps: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, look back. docs.section: “Done” has to be something a machine can check
docs.text: “Make it work” is not a definition of done. “Make it work” is not a definition of done. “Make it look nice” is worse. Without a runnable check, the agent stops when the work looks finished — and you become the test suite. Write the check into the request. Three tests that must pass. A command that must exit cleanly. A number you worked out by hand that the screen must match. Claude Code’s /goal command re-checks a condition after every turn; phrase it so the agent’s own output proves it — npm test exiting 0, git status coming back clean ( /goal docs ). docs.text: It will be wrong, confidently, in front of you. It will be wrong, confidently, in front of you. Kent Beck lists three signals to take the wheel back: it loops, it adds functionality nobody asked for, and it cheats — disabling or deleting tests to get a green result ( Augmented Coding, 25 Jun 2025 ). Disagreeing well is a technique, not a mood: Bring evidence, not adjectives. “This is wrong” gives it nothing. “I ran npm test , here is the output, line 14 expected 2 and got 11” gives it the whole problem. Say what you expected and what you saw. Two sentences. Most bad agent output is a correct answer to a question you did not ask. Ask it to explain before it edits. “Explain in three sentences why this happens, then wait.” If the explanation is nonsense, the fix would have been too. docs.text: The docs page tells the agent the contract. The docs page tells the agent the contract. A real response tells it the truth. docs.text: You do not need a testing framework. You do not need a testing framework. A check is anything the agent can run that comes back yes or no. The Claude Code guide lists the usual ones: a test suite, the build exit code, a linter, a script that diffs your output against a fixture, a browser screenshot compared against a design. Four ways to make the agent obey a check, in rising order of setup: Ask in the prompt. “Run npm test and keep going until it passes. Show me the output.” Free, and it usually works. /goal <condition> . Claude Code runs a separate small model that re-checks your condition after every turn. A Stop hook. A script that will not let the turn end until your command exits zero. Claude Code overrides it after eight consecutive blocks, so it is a strong nudge, not a cage. A verification subagent — a fresh model whose only job is to try to refute the result. Two rules from the same page. Ask for evidence — the command and its output — not assertions. If you cannot verify it, do not ship it. ! The agent is not lying to you “All tests pass” can be true and useless at once. T

docs.section: What to test first when you have no tests
docs.text: The classic picture is a pyramid, and it shows why your instincts are usually upside down. The classic picture is a pyramid, and it shows why your instincts are usually upside down. Cheap and precise at the bottom, slow and truthful at the top. Your first test belongs at the top; everything after it pushes downward. That is where you end up after a year, not where you start. With zero tests, write one test at the top: the single path your product exists for. For QAIRU Event Sign-up that is open the page, fill in a name and an email, press reserve, see a confirmation . Then push downward and let the bugs choose. Every time something breaks, that bug becomes a unit test before it becomes a fix. Anthropic’s bug-fix pattern is the same: describe the symptom, the likely location and what “fixed” means, ask for a failing test that reproduces it, then the fix. Your suite fills with real failures, not imagined ones.

docs.title: Make the Agent Prove It
docs.section: Write the test that fails, then let it code
docs.text: Red/green TDD fits agents better than it ever fit humans. Red/green TDD fits agents better than it ever fit humans. Simon Willison’s one-line version: add “Use red/green TDD” to a build prompt. The agent writes the test, watches it fail, then implements until it passes ( Agentic Engineering Patterns ). The red step is the part people skip, and the part that carries the value. A test you never saw fail might pass for the wrong reason: it may assert nothing, or keep passing after you delete the feature. Red first is the proof that it is wired to the behaviour it checks. Four reasons it suits an agent: The loop closes without you. The agent runs the test, reads the failure, iterates. You no longer stand between attempt one and attempt two. It bounds the work. Red/green guards against code that does not work and against extra code nobody asked for. The test is the edge of the task. It survives the session. The next session starts with no memory of this one. The test does not. The agent optimises for whatever you measure. Anthropic built a C compiler with sixteen parallel Claude instances

docs.section: Reading the diff it just handed you
docs.text: Nobody here is clean. Treat it as a direction, not a measurement. Five things to look for in an AI diff, in this order. Does it do what you asked? Not “does it look reasonable” — does it meet the requirement. Name the one it misses. Would the tests fail if the feature broke? Delete the feature mentally and ask which test goes red. If none, the tests are decoration. Was anything swallowed? An empty catch , a default that hides a missing case, a try that turns a crash into silence. This failure reaches production and never shows up in a log. Does this code already exist? Duplication is the clearest signal in the numbers above, and the easiest to catch — you just have to ask. What changed that you did not ask for? Scope creep is common in agent diffs, and it is where risk hides. Input validation, auth checks and secrets in code go on this list too; the rest is module 11 . ❯ Adversarial self-review of the diff Claude Code · fresh session (/clear first) Copy You are reviewing a change you did not write. Start by reading it: `git diff main...HEAD`. Your job is to find what is wrong with it

Tests: which of these tests would still pass if I deleted the feature entirely? List them by name. Was any test skipped, weakened, or deleted in this diff? 4. Show me both copies with file and line. 6. Scope: anything changed that the task did not require? For each finding give: file and line, what breaks, a concrete failing scenario, a fix. docs.section: Plan mode: argue with the plan, not the diff
docs.text: In plan mode the agent reads and explores but cannot touch your source. In plan mode the agent reads and explores but cannot touch your source. It comes back with a plan; Ctrl+G opens it in your editor so you can rewrite it before approving. One constraint added to a plan costs a sentence. The same constraint pulled out of finished code costs an afternoon. On approval you pick: auto mode, manual approval of each edit, or “No, keep planning”. The shape is explore, plan, implement, commit. Skip the plan when you could describe the diff in one sentence — a typo, a rename, a log line. Plan when the approach is uncertain, the change spans files, or the code is new to both of you.

docs.section: What it loads before you type
docs.text: CLAUDE.md is read whole at the start of every session, broad to specific: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, then… CLAUDE.md is read whole at the start of every session, broad to specific: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md , then ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md , then a gitignored ./CLAUDE.local.md . Since v2.1.277 Claude Code also reads a repo’s AGENTS.md when no CLAUDE.md exists — the file Codex, Cursor, Copilot and Jules read too. What goes inside it is module 06 . Two things matter here: under 200 lines, because bloat makes rules get ignored; and it is context, not enforcement — to truly block something, use a deny rule or a hook. Everything shares one context window, and quality drops as it fills ( module 02 ). Four commands: /context shows what is eating the window, /clear starts a fresh conversation for free, /compact keep the API decisions and the file list summarises on your terms, /btw what does localStorage do? asks a side question that stays out of the history. The docs’ rule: corrected it twice on the same thing? /clear and write a better prompt.

docs.section: Rewind is local undo. Git is real undo.
docs.text: Every prompt that starts a turn creates a checkpoint. Every prompt that starts a turn creates a checkpoint. Esc Esc on an empty input (or /rewind ) opens the menu: restore code and conversation, restore one, or summarise part of the session. The last 100 per session are kept; snapshots are swept after about 30 days. Checkpoints track edits made by Claude’s own edit tools. They do not track files changed by Bash commands, most subagent edits, your own manual edits, or anything remote — a database write, a deploy, a push. That is the whole argument for git init and a commit before you let an agent run ( module 09 ). Quick check The agent ran a shell command that deleted a folder, including a file you still needed. What actually gets it back? A Esc Esc, then "Restore code" — checkpoints cover every change made during the session B /compact, which rebuilds the session state from its summary C A git commit you made before the run — checkpoints do not track files changed by Bash commands D /context, which reloads the files that were in the window

docs.section: Four ways to teach it once
docs.text: Skills are a folder with a SKILL.md in .claude/skills/<name>/. Skills are a folder with a SKILL.md in .claude/skills/<name>/ . Only the description sits in context; the body loads when needed. That is why a skill beats another page bolted onto CLAUDE.md. Call it as /name , or let the agent pick it up when the description matches. It follows the open Agent Skills standard, so skills are not Claude-only. Subagents are helpers with their own context window, tools and permissions. They do the noisy work — searching a big repo, reading a log — and return a summary, so the mess lands in their window, not yours. Explore, Plan and general-purpose are built in; yours live in .claude/agents/<name>.md . /rewind usually does not restore their edits. Hooks are your own shell commands, run at lifecycle events: PreToolUse (exit code 2 blocks the action), PostToolUse , Stop , Notification . Unlike a line in CLAUDE.md, a hook always fires — the difference between “please run the formatter” and a formatter that runs. MCP plugs external tools and data into an agent — issue trackers, databases, browsers

docs.text: He asked for changes as small as “decrease the padding on the sidebar by half” — finding the line himself was… The post went out at 23:17 UTC on Sunday 2 February 2025 — 04:17 Monday morning here. It was not a methodology. It was a habit: Cursor Composer and Sonnet, dictating into SuperWhisper, barely touching the keyboard. His instruction to himself, in his own words: “forget that the code even exists”. He asked for changes as small as “decrease the padding on the sidebar by half” — finding the line himself was more effort than asking. He accepted every diff unread. When something broke, he pasted the error back with no comment, and usually that was enough. The code grew past what he could hold in his head. Bugs he could not fix, he worked around or attacked with random changes until they went away. Then the sentence almost nobody quotes: “It’s not too bad for throwaway weekend projects”. docs.text: Something changed at the end of 2025. Something changed at the end of 2025. Karpathy’s own account is unusually specific. In November he was at roughly 80% manual and autocomplete coding, 20% agents. By December it had flipped to 80% agent coding , 20% edits and touch-ups. On 26 December 2025 he wrote that he had never felt this far behind as a programmer. Remember that the next time you feel lost in this course. On 4 February 2026, a year and two days after the original, he posted a retrospective. Vibe coding made sense when models were weak and the whole thing was for fun. By 2026, programming through agents was becoming the default professional workflow, with real oversight and no trade against quality. That needed a different name. His current favourite is “agentic engineering”. “Agentic” because “you are not writing the code directly 99% of the time”. “Engineering” because there is “an art & science and expertise to it” — meaning it can be taught, which is the premise of this masterclass. Tokens in — your prompt, your files, every tool result, and the entire conversation so far — and tokens out, which is what it writes back. Prices on this page are USD per million tokens at the standard non-batch, non-cached rate. Output is the expensive meter everywhere: 4 to 6 times input across every vendor here, because input is read in a single pass while output has to be produced one token at a time. You might conclude that output dominates your bill, and for a chatbot it does. For a coding agent it does not, because the agent re-sends its whole context on every single turn of the loop, so a long session is mostly input, read over and over.
